limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- Covenant levels are not printed in any of the five filings, so headroom against the minimum fixed charge coverage and maximum lease-adjusted leverage tests cannot be calculated, which restricts every covenant conclusion (High); the credit agreement and a compliance computation would close it. - The company states no EBITDA or adjusted EBITDA and states its own transaction-adjusted net leverage only for the ends of 2024 and 2025, so EBITDA is derived for every period and the September 2026 company figure is not established (Medium); earnings releases or the credit-agreement computation would close it. - The FY2025 net cash change is withheld because the three printed activity totals add to a decrease of USD 28.9 million while the filing prints USD 29.0 million, a rounding difference of USD 0.1 million (Low); the opening and closing cash agree. - Total liabilities for FY2024 and FY2025 are withheld because the statement prints no total and the printed liability lines are USD 0.1 million short of total assets less equity in both years (Low); the September 2026 figure is the sum of printed lines. - The maturity ladder is drawn at December 31, 2025 and the September 2026 quarterly report prints no maturity schedule, so principal due from 2027 onward cannot be restated at September 30, 2026, and only current maturities of USD 439.2 million are known (Medium); the next schedule would close it. - Revolver availability of USD 794.3 million is USD 109.9 million below the commitment less letters of credit and drawings, and the filings do not say whether borrowing-base limits or conversions to floor plan explain it (Medium); the credit agreement would close it. - Lines printed as a dash in a statement are treated as not supplied rather than zero: asset impairments for the third quarter of 2026, real estate capital expenditure for nine months 2025, acquisitions for nine months 2026, several financing lines in the years where they are absent, and liabilities held for sale at September 30, 2026 (Low); the effect on any total is nil because the totals are as printed. - Floor plan interest paid is split only for fiscal years, so cash interest cover excluding floor plan interest cannot be built for the twelve months to September 2026 (Low). - The revolving credit facility, the floor plan facilities and the finance lease are left out of the debt stack because no source states their legal rank or security (Medium); the credit agreement would close it. - Deferred income taxes and several other lines are absent from the interim cash flow statements and are shown as not supplied for the nine-month columns (Low).

citations.quote: Asbury's diversified franchise network, owned real estate and service-led gross profit give creditors a durable business, but softening vehicle margins and debt-funded expansion leave less room for error than the scale suggests.

facts.label: Bottom line
facts.text: Parts and service earned 47.9% of FY2025 gross profit on 13.9% of revenue, which cushions weaker new vehicle margins, and 83.0% of dealership locations were owned at the end of 2025. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a durable-business view is the 2026 earnings trend. Nine-month income from operations fell 16% to USD 620.0 million, gross profit per new vehicle in the third quarter fell 12% to USD 2,949, and selling, general and administrative expense reached 68.6% of gross profit against 64.0% a year earlier, so the cost base is not flexing as fast as profit. The company's leverage target is 2.5x to 3.5x on its own definition, and the funding of the Herb Chambers purchase and of buybacks with borrowings and sale proceeds leaves less slack if margins keep falling. The view would strengthen if selling, general and administrative expense returned toward the FY2025 share of 64.7% of gross profit, new vehicle gross profit per unit stabilised, the December 2026 real estate facility were refinanced on committed terms and buybacks stayed paused while leverage is above target. It would weaken if the FTC refiled, a manufacturer exercised change-of-control or termination rights, or buybacks resumed with debt. facts.label: Bottom line
facts.text: The strongest support is a profit base in which parts and service earned 47.9% of FY2025 gross profit, owned real estate and company-defined liquidity of USD 1,031.9 million. The main constraints are twelve-month EBITDA of USD 838.6 million, interest cover of 2.93x, a USD 401.7 million real estate loan due in December 2026 whose refinancing is not yet documented, and covenant levels that no filing prints. The primary downside path runs from weaker new vehicle margins through a cost base that does not flex to higher leverage and thinner cover. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The initiating condition is a further softening of new vehicle demand and margins from higher prices and weaker affordability, as in the third quarter of 2026 when new vehicle gross profit fell 20%. The first operational break is gross profit per new vehicle; because personnel, rent and system costs do not fall in step, income from operations and EBITDA drop faster than revenue. If EBITDA fell again by the USD 104.4 million already lost since year-end with net debt unchanged, net leverage would rise from 3.92x to 4.47x and interest cover would fall from 2.93x to 2.56x. Management levers are to keep buybacks paused against USD 322.4 million of remaining authorization, trim capital expenditure from the USD 250.0 million to USD 275.0 million plan, and sell further stores as it did for USD 397.2 million in nine months 2026. Company-defined liquidity of USD 1,031.9 million is 2.57 times the December 2026 maturity of USD 401.7 million, so a liquidity crisis does not appear likely within twelve months, but covenant headroom at the higher leverage cannot be established. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Asbury presents an adequate business profile supported by a service-led profit mix, brand and regional breadth and owned property, but credit quality is constrained by falling earnings, net leverage of 3.92x and a nearest maturity of USD 401.7 million that is not yet refinanced. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because parts and service and finance and insurance supply most gross profit, although free cash flow is lower than a year ago. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on the willingness of real estate lenders and the bank group to renew secured and floor plan lines, and on noteholders in 2028 to 2030. The primary downside path is margin compression in new vehicles feeding through a fixed cost base into leverage and cover. Further analysis would require the credit agreement and covenant levels, the company's leverage computation for September 2026, ratings and market prices, and any financing completed after October 30, 2026. Completed. Top risk: earnings decline on a largely fixed cost base while refinancing is pending. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C1; calculation C5; calculation C6

## Findings
### Bottom line

The five filings support a credit snapshot of Asbury Automotive Group as of September 30, 2026, but covenant headroom, ratings and market pricing cannot be assessed from them. Creditors can rely on the consolidated statements, the full debt schedule and the stated liquidity; they cannot rely on covenant levels, which no document prints.

The set runs from the 2024 annual report to the quarterly report signed on October 30, 2026, which is 19 days before the as-of date. Every document is a primary filing by the registrant. No executed credit agreement, indenture, rating report, lender presentation or market quote was supplied, and the filings give no EBITDA figure of the company's own, so earnings power has to be rebuilt from statement lines. The 2021 real estate facility matures in December 2026, after the latest evidence, and its refinancing is not documented in the set.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 56, 66; calculation C1

spans.text: ## Request

Financial foundation for Asbury Automotive Group Inc (issuer abg-1144980) as of 2026-11-18 on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is the consolidated statements, debt, cash, liquidity and credit ratios of the registrant for FY2024, FY2025 and the nine months to September 30, 2026, taken from the five supplied filings.
## Sources
| Source | Document | Document date | sha256 | Use |

| 10-K_2024-12-31_abg_abg-20241231.htm.jsonl | Annual report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2024 | 2025-02-26 (date of the registrant's signature) | c0f85975876733a38ac8c4c9a53391af74c4566da948223d619a78ba1a1c9e67 | Tie-out of FY2024 comparatives, FY2024 liquidity statement and floor plan interest paid |

| 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl | Annual report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025 | 2026-02-20 (date of the registrant's signature) | 51718e50cf3bbd267b1533309c3b354cd5146560d81b3f1f6ff06a25bbeb282e | FY2024 and FY2025 statements, debt note, maturities, leases, interest paid, covenant wording |

| 10-Q_2026-03-31_abg_abg-20260331.htm.jsonl | Quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the period ended March 31, 2026 | 2026-05-01 (date of the registrant's signature) | e8cb17d6cfc8aef7ca56701027e2c4e79f8e47007c050525b910558158b169d9 | Stated liquidity at March 31, 2026 |

| Handoff module | Plain name | sha256 | Use |
| CP-0 | Source readiness | f39d412f5b78e57c3d05dca5a53c8a2f1a0d897a79aef8c2ee93a0d425b2e49f | Source coverage, perimeter, gaps on covenant levels, company EBITDA and lease table labels |
## Findings
### Bottom line

Leverage on reported earnings rose to 3.92x net debt to EBITDA at September 30, 2026 from 3.75x at the end of 2025, and interest cover fell to 2.93x from 3.43x, so creditors have a thinner earnings cushion even though liquidity improved.

Debt did not rise: net debt fell by USD 246.5 million over nine months as dealership sale proceeds came in, but last-twelve-month EBITDA fell by USD 104.4 million. Charging floor plan interest against earnings lifts net leverage to 4.38x. The company's own year-end ratio of 3.2x cannot be extended to September 2026 because none is stated for that date, and covenant levels are not printed.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 5–6, 55–56; 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 14, 96; calculation C2; calculation C4; calculation C7; calculation C9; calculation C10
### Leverage and coverage

The reading depends on which earnings and which debt are used. Net debt to EBITDA, with EBITDA built from income from operations plus depreciation and amortization, was 3.37x at the end of 2024, 3.75x at the end of 2025 and 3.92x for the twelve months to September 30, 2026; total debt to EBITDA was 3.45x, 3.79x and 4.02x. Interest cover on total cash interest paid, floor plan interest included, was 3.38x, 3.43x and 2.93x. The weakening comes from lower earnings: twelve-month EBITDA of USD 838.6 million compares with USD 943.0 million for FY2025, while net debt of USD 3,285.1 million is below the USD 3,531.6 million at year end.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 96, 98–99, 131; 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3, 5–6; calculation C1; calculation C2; calculation C3; calculation C4; calculation C5; calculation C6; calculation C7; calculation C10

Adding back asset impairments, a non-cash charge of USD 141.0 million in FY2025, brings FY2025 net leverage to 3.26x and the twelve months to September 2026 to 3.43x; the first is close to the company's own transaction-adjusted ratio of 3.2x at the end of 2025, which the filing says is calculated as set out in its credit facility and which cannot be reproduced here. Treating floor plan interest as a cost of the business instead lifts net leverage to 3.74x for FY2024, 4.15x for FY2025 and 4.38x for the twelve months to September 2026. Floor plan interest of USD 91.2 million in FY2025 is charged below income from operations, so EBITDA before it flatters the cover of the debt that is counted. No covenant level is printed, so none of these figures can be set against a breach point.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 14, 96; 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 56; calculation C8; calculation C9
### Cash flow quality

Operating cash flow held up better than earnings but is not a clean measure, because trade floor plan changes sit inside it and non-trade floor plan flows sit in financing. Reported operating cash flow was USD 617.7 million for nine months 2026 against USD 623.3 million a year earlier; the company's own adjusted measure that brings floor plan flows into operations was USD 525.2 million against USD 542.6 million. Capital expenditure including real estate was USD 248.0 million, up from USD 104.4 million, leaving USD 369.7 million of free cash flow on the reported measure, against USD 518.9 million in the prior nine months.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6, 58–59; calculation C14

Dealership sale proceeds of USD 397.2 million and share repurchases of USD 277.6 million were the largest other items, so the fall in net debt rests on divestitures as well as on operations. Repurchases were USD 50.0 million in the prior nine months; the authorization has USD 322.4 million remaining, and the filings state that buybacks and dividends are subject to covenant compliance.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6, 9, 56
### Liquidity and maturities

Stated liquidity of USD 1.03 billion at September 30, 2026 compares with USD 927.1 million at the end of 2025, but USD 160.6 million of the total is cash held in floor plan offset accounts and USD 38.9 million of balance-sheet cash sits in the insurance subsidiary outside the guarantor group, so the cash and facilities that are freely available to the debt holders are smaller than the headline. Revolver availability of USD 794.3 million is USD 109.9 million below the commitment less letters of credit and drawings, and the filing does not explain the gap. Principal falling due is concentrated in 2026 (USD 484.4 million at year-end 2025, including the 2021 real estate facility of USD 401.7 million that matures in December 2026 and that management expects to refinance) and in 2028 to 2030, with USD 610.2 million, USD 837.7 million and USD 482.9 million.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 74, 131; 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 18–19, 55–56; calculation C12; calculation C15
### Definitions and data quality

Four definitions move the leverage figures. Floor plan notes payable of USD 1,764.3 million at September 30, 2026 and loaner vehicle notes of USD 250.4 million sit outside total debt, which is the carrying value of current and long-term debt only; deferred revenue of USD 891.3 million is a non-debt funding float that has grown from USD 828.2 million at the end of 2025; the cash figure includes the insurance subsidiary's cash; and carrying value at year-end 2025 is USD 21.4 million below contractual principal because of issuance costs net of premiums. The statements also print small rounding differences, so FY2025 net cash change and FY2024 and FY2025 total liabilities are withheld rather than forced.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 12, 18–19; 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 96, 98–99, 131; calculation C11; calculation C13; calculation C18; calculation C19

## Gaps

- Covenant levels are not printed in any of the five filings, so headroom against the minimum fixed charge coverage and maximum lease-adjusted leverage tests cannot be calculated, which restricts every covenant conclusion (High); the credit agreement and a compliance computation would close it.

- The company states no EBITDA or adjusted EBITDA and states its own transaction-adjusted net leverage only for the ends of 2024 and 2025, so EBITDA is derived for every period and the September 2026 company figure is not established (Medium); earnings releases or the credit-agreement computation would close it.

- The FY2025 net cash change is withheld because the three printed activity totals add to a decrease of USD 28.9 million while the filing prints USD 29.0 million, a rounding difference of USD 0.1 million (Low); the opening and closing cash agree.

- Total liabilities for FY2024 and FY2025 are withheld because the statement prints no total and the printed liability lines are USD 0.1 million short of total assets less equity in both years (Low); the September 2026 figure is the sum of printed lines.

- The maturity ladder is drawn at December 31, 2025 and the September 2026 quarterly report prints no maturity schedule, so principal due from 2027 onward cannot be restated at September 30, 2026, and only current maturities of USD 439.2 million are known (Medium); the next schedule would close it.

- Revolver availability of USD 794.3 million is USD 109.9 million below the commitment less letters of credit and drawings, and the filings do not say whether borrowing-base limits or conversions to floor plan explain it (Medium); the credit agreement would close it.

- Lines printed as a dash in a statement are treated as not supplied rather than zero: asset impairments for the third quarter of 2026, real estate capital expenditure for nine months 2025, acquisitions for nine months 2026, several financing lines in the years where they are absent, and liabilities held for sale at September 30, 2026 (Low); the effect on any total is nil because the totals are as printed.
- Floor plan interest paid is split only for fiscal years, so cash interest cover excluding floor plan interest cannot be built for the twelve months to September 2026 (Low).

- The revolving credit facility, the floor plan facilities and the finance lease are left out of the debt stack because no source states their legal rank or security (Medium); the credit agreement would close it.
- Deferred income taxes and several other lines are absent from the interim cash flow statements and are shown as not supplied for the nine-month columns (Low).

## Findings
### Bottom line

Asbury's diversified franchise network, owned real estate and service-led gross profit give creditors a durable business, but softening vehicle margins and debt-funded expansion leave less room for error than the scale suggests.

Parts and service earned 47.9% of FY2025 gross profit on 13.9% of revenue, which cushions weaker new vehicle margins, and 83.0% of dealership locations were owned at the end of 2025. The Herb Chambers purchase of USD 1,761.8 million in July 2025 was funded entirely by floor plan, revolver and real estate borrowings, and since then nine-month income from operations has fallen while share repurchases reached USD 277.6 million. A controls weakness at the end of 2024 was remediated, but the acquired stores were outside the 2025 controls assessment.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 55, 64, 116, 161–162; 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 12, 56; calculation C1; calculation C3
### Key findings

Franchise and brand breadth limits dependence on any one manufacturer or region, although one manufacturer group is still the largest single exposure. Toyota and Lexus supplied 30% of FY2025 new vehicle revenue and Ford and Lincoln 14%, and the new vehicle mix for the nine months to September 2026 was 41% imports, 33% luxury and 26% domestic. After divestitures the group runs 34 brands in 14 states, against 36 brands in 15 states at the end of 2025.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 9–10, 32; 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 7

Profit depends on service and finance and insurance rather than vehicle sales, which stabilises earnings but does not remove the new vehicle squeeze. Parts and service earned 47.9% of FY2025 gross profit and finance and insurance 23.4%, while new vehicles earned 20.2% on 52.8% of revenue. In the nine months to September 2026 new vehicle gross profit fell 15%, a USD 68.4 million drop, while parts and service gross profit rose 2%.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 64; 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 45–46; calculation C1; calculation C4

The July 2025 Herb Chambers purchase bought scale and Northeast presence with debt secured on real estate and inventory, and management has since sold stores for cash. Of the USD 1,761.8 million price, 33.6% came from floor plan facilities, 35.4% from the revolver and 31.0% from a USD 546.5 million real estate term loan; the stores added USD 1.80 billion of revenue and USD 43.3 million of net income in nine months 2026. Dealership sales raised USD 397.2 million in the same nine months at a gain of USD 126.4 million, which indicates active pruning of the portfolio rather than expansion alone.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 12–15; calculation C2

Owned real estate gives asset backing but puts secured lenders ahead of noteholders on the financed properties. At the end of 2025, 83.0% of dealership locations were owned; the real estate term loans carry first-priority liens on the properties they financed, while the senior notes are unsecured and guaranteed by every restricted subsidiary except the TCA entities.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 55, 86, 134–139; calculation C3

Governance risk is medium, not low: there is no sponsor, no dividend since 2008 and no related-party distribution disclosed in the supplied filings, but buybacks have been large, manufacturers hold change-of-control rights and a new chief executive has signed the reports since mid-2026. The buyback authorization was raised to USD 500.0 million in February 2026 with USD 322.4 million remaining at September 30, 2026, and no repurchases were made in the third quarter.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 18, 58; 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9, 56, 66; 10-Q_2026-06-30_abg_abg-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 65; Source readiness (CP-0)

Reporting quality has improved but is not clean. The material weakness in controls over the dealer management system vendor of the Koons stores was remediated during 2025, yet management's assessment excluded the Herb Chambers stores, which held USD 1.89 billion of total assets, and 47 stores moved to a new dealer system in the third quarter of 2026.

Legal exposure has eased but is not closed. The FTC dismissed its administrative proceeding on October 5, 2026 and keeps the ability to refile, and the company's own lawsuit against the FTC is still pending; the filings give no estimate of loss for this matter.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 56; 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 27
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a durable-business view is the 2026 earnings trend. Nine-month income from operations fell 16% to USD 620.0 million, gross profit per new vehicle in the third quarter fell 12% to USD 2,949, and selling, general and administrative expense reached 68.6% of gross profit against 64.0% a year earlier, so the cost base is not flexing as fast as profit. The company's leverage target is 2.5x to 3.5x on its own definition, and the funding of the Herb Chambers purchase and of buybacks with borrowings and sale proceeds leaves less slack if margins keep falling. The view would strengthen if selling, general and administrative expense returned toward the FY2025 share of 64.7% of gross profit, new vehicle gross profit per unit stabilised, the December 2026 real estate facility were refinanced on committed terms and buybacks stayed paused while leverage is above target. It would weaken if the FTC refiled, a manufacturer exercised change-of-control or termination rights, or buybacks resumed with debt.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 37, 54, 56; 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 14, 72; calculation C4
### Limitations

- Ownership percentages, board composition and related-party dealings sit in a proxy statement that was not supplied, so the conclusion that no holder controls financial policy rests on the absence of any disclosed holder, not on an ownership table.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 163; Source readiness (CP-0)

- The filings do not name the counterparty of the August 2026 consulting agreement or the role of the executive under the September 2026 severance agreement, so the view on management continuity rests on signatures and exhibit titles only.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 65–66
- The Mercedes-Benz Boston put right described when the Herb Chambers agreement was signed is not mentioned in later filings, so any contingent purchase obligation is not established.
Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_abg_abg-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 165

- No document dated after October 30, 2026 was supplied, so the expected December 2026 refinancing and any other late-year change in portfolio or leadership are management expectation or not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 56, 66
- Revenue by state is not tabulated in the filings, so regional concentration beyond the brand and state footprint cannot be measured.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 7–10

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

The defining transaction is the Herb Chambers acquisition, agreed on February 14, 2025 and completed on July 21, 2025 for a final purchase price of USD 1,761.8 million. It added 33 dealerships, 52 franchises and three collision centers and was funded by USD 292.0 million of new vehicle floor plan financing, USD 300.0 million of used vehicle financing, USD 623.3 million of revolver borrowings and a USD 546.5 million ten-year real estate term loan. The signing note had estimated USD 1.34 billion before vehicles, parts and reimbursements, so the final price is higher than the first estimate because vehicles, parts and reimbursements were priced at closing.

The only new debt in the period is that purchase financing: the April 9, 2025 amendment raised the revolver commitment from USD 500.0 million to USD 925.0 million and the new vehicle floor plan facility from USD 1.93 billion to USD 2.25 billion, and the July 21, 2025 real estate loan funded the stores and their property. No new senior notes were issued in the period, and the nearest large maturity is the 2021 real estate facility, scheduled for December 2026 with refinancing expected by management.

Divestitures run the other way: the company sold 24 franchises for USD 566.5 million in FY2025 and 19 franchises for USD 397.2 million in the nine months to September 2026, of which 14 franchises were sold in the first quarter of 2026 for USD 361.5 million at a gain of USD 125.8 million. One franchise and one real estate property were held for sale at September 30, 2026.

spans.text: ## Request

Fundamental credit for Asbury Automotive Group Inc (issuer abg-1144980) as of 2026-11-18 on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is the overall credit profile, its strongest support, its weakest dimension and the primary downside path, built from the Financial foundation, Business & governance and Source readiness analyses and the five supplied public filings.
## Sources

## Findings
### Bottom line

Asbury's franchise network and service-led profits support a fundamentally sound credit, but net debt of 3.92x EBITDA and falling interest cover leave noteholders with a thinner cushion until earnings stabilise.

The strongest support is a profit base in which parts and service earned 47.9% of FY2025 gross profit, owned real estate and company-defined liquidity of USD 1,031.9 million. The main constraints are twelve-month EBITDA of USD 838.6 million, interest cover of 2.93x, a USD 401.7 million real estate loan due in December 2026 whose refinancing is not yet documented, and covenant levels that no filing prints. The primary downside path runs from weaker new vehicle margins through a cost base that does not flex to higher leverage and thinner cover.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 55–56; calculation C1; calculation C2; calculation C4; calculation C5; calculation C6
### Key findings

The business profile is a strength: scale, brand and regional breadth, and a profit mix tilted to service. Parts and service earned 47.9% of FY2025 gross profit and finance and insurance 23.4%, while new vehicles earned 20.2% on 52.8% of revenue, so earnings are steadier than vehicle revenue implies, and 83.0% of dealership locations were owned at the end of 2025.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C6

Earnings are the weak point. Twelve-month EBITDA of USD 838.6 million is USD 104.4 million below the FY2025 figure of USD 943.0 million, because selling, general and administrative expense rose to 68.6% of gross profit from 64.0% while new vehicle gross profit per unit fell. The cost base follows commissions down but not fast enough to protect the margin.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 45, 54; calculation C2; calculation C9

Leverage is elevated against the company's own target and its own reported ratio. Net debt to EBITDA was 3.92x and total debt to EBITDA 4.02x for the twelve months to September 2026, against a company target of 2.5x to 3.5x on its own definition and a reported 3.2x at the end of 2025; treating floor plan interest as a cost lifts net leverage to 4.38x. Debt itself fell, so the deterioration is an earnings problem, not a borrowing problem.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 14; calculation C1; calculation C7

Coverage and cash generation are adequate but narrowing. Interest cover on total cash interest paid was 2.93x against 3.43x at the end of 2025, and nine-month free cash flow after capital expenditure of USD 248.0 million was USD 369.7 million against USD 518.9 million a year earlier, with share repurchases of USD 277.6 million and dealership sale proceeds of USD 397.2 million the largest other items.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C1; calculation C3; calculation C8

Liquidity is adequate and refinancing capacity depends on secured real estate lenders and bank facilities. The company reports total available liquidity of USD 1.03 billion, which its components add to USD 1,031.9 million, of which USD 160.6 million is floor plan offset cash; counted on a stricter basis, cash and committed facilities are USD 905.9 million. The December 2026 real estate facility of USD 401.7 million is the nearest large maturity, and the 2028 to 2030 maturities are USD 610.2 million, USD 837.7 million and USD 482.9 million.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 55–56; calculation C4; calculation C5; calculation C13

Financial policy is mixed rather than conservative. There is no dividend, no sponsor and buybacks paused in the third quarter, but the authorization was raised to USD 500.0 million in February 2026 and the debt-funded Herb Chambers purchase added secured and floor plan borrowings; the reporting weakness at the end of 2024 was remediated while the acquired stores were excluded from the 2025 controls assessment.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9; calculation C8

Structure favors secured lenders on the properties they financed and leaves noteholders exposed to value outside them. The real estate term loans, USD 1,129.4 million in principal with the mortgage notes, carry first-priority liens, while the four senior notes are unsecured and guaranteed by every restricted subsidiary except the insurance and F&I entities.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C10
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case for a better view is that the company's own measure is within target, that parts and service gross profit is still rising, that no repurchases were made in the third quarter, that company-defined liquidity improved from USD 927.1 million at the end of 2025 to USD 1,031.9 million, and that net debt fell by USD 246.5 million over nine months. Twelve-month EBITDA before impairments of USD 957.8 million would put net leverage at 3.43x, inside the target range. The view would improve if selling, general and administrative expense moved back toward 64.7% of gross profit, new vehicle gross profit per unit stabilised, the December 2026 loan were refinanced on committed terms and the credit agreement showed ample headroom. It would worsen if a further EBITDA decline of the size already seen, USD 104.4 million, took net leverage to 4.47x and cover to 2.56x, if buybacks resumed with borrowings, or if a refinancing slipped past December.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 54, 56; calculation C2; calculation C7; calculation C11
### Limitations
- Covenant levels are not printed, so the conclusion on debt service and distribution capacity rests on the company's statement of compliance and cannot be tested against a breach point.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 56; Source readiness (CP-0)
- Earnings are built from statement lines because the company states no EBITDA, so the comparison with its own 3.2x ratio is indicative and the September 2026 company ratio is not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 14
- The maturity schedule is drawn at the end of 2025, so the maturity wall after 2026 is not restated for nine months of repayments and sales.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 131
- The filings give no management projections beyond capital expenditure and the tax rate, and no rating or market price, so the outlook and market-access judgements are qualitative.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 55, 60; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Strengths and weaknesses

The first strength is a service-led profit base that has held up while vehicle sales weakened: parts and service gross profit rose 2% in the nine months to September 2026 while new vehicle gross profit fell 15%, so the largest profit pool is the one that is growing, which supports cash flow visibility and debt service.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 45; calculation C6; calculation C9

The second strength is breadth: 34 brands in 14 states and no single manufacturer above 30% of new vehicle revenue spread franchise, regional and model-cycle risk, which limits the chance that one supplier decision removes a large share of earnings.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 32

The third strength is asset backing: 83.0% of dealership locations are owned and the real estate term loans and mortgage notes total USD 1,129.4 million, so there is tangible collateral behind secured debt and a funding source for stores that are sold or relocated.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C6; calculation C10

The fourth strength is company-defined liquidity of USD 1,031.9 million with no revolver drawn, which covers the nearest large maturity of USD 401.7 million more than twice over on the company's own total and on a stricter basis.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 55; calculation C4; calculation C12

The fifth strength is a plain financial policy: no sponsor, no dividend since 2008 and a pause in buybacks in the third quarter, which keeps distributions within management's discretion and out of any lender-adverse structure.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9

The first weakness is falling earnings with a sticky cost base: selling, general and administrative expense rose to 68.6% of gross profit from 64.0% and income from operations fell 16% to USD 620.0 million, so each further point of gross profit lost reaches EBITDA almost in full.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 45, 54; calculation C9

The second weakness is leverage above where the company's own target sits: net debt was 3.92x twelve-month EBITDA, 4.38x if floor plan interest is a cost, against a target of 2.5x to 3.5x and a reported 3.2x at the end of 2025, which uses most of the room that the target leaves for a shock.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 14; calculation C1; calculation C7

The third weakness is refinancing concentration: USD 401.7 million falls due in December 2026 with refinancing expected but undocumented, and USD 610.2 million, USD 837.7 million and USD 482.9 million fall due in 2028 to 2030, so lender appetite for secured real estate and senior notes in those years determines whether debt can be rolled.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 56; calculation C5

The fourth weakness is opacity of lender protections: no covenant level, definition or compliance figure is printed and no executed agreement is supplied, so headroom against a minimum fixed charge coverage test and a maximum lease-adjusted leverage test cannot be measured.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0); 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 56

The fifth weakness is distribution and acquisition appetite combined with integration risk: buybacks of USD 277.6 million in nine months 2026 followed a USD 1,761.8 million debt-funded acquisition whose stores were outside the 2025 controls assessment, so policy can move faster than controls and earnings.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C8
### Company and ownership

Asbury is a franchised retailer of new and used vehicles with parts and service and finance and insurance, operated through wholly owned subsidiaries under a public holding company with no sponsor or controlling holder identified in the supplied filings. Cash flow visibility comes from repeat service work and manufacturer-backed warranty and recall repairs, while the main structural dependence is on manufacturer relationships: Toyota and Lexus supplied 30% of FY2025 new vehicle revenue, and dealer agreements give manufacturers consent and termination rights on control changes, which limits recapitalisation risk but exposes the franchises to any large holder.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 17–18, 32
### Revenue, cost and cash conversion

Revenue depends on new vehicle volume, which is cyclical and discretionary, and on price and mix: Q3 2026 new vehicle units fell 9% and the seasonally adjusted annual sales rate eased to about 16.4 million from 16.6 million, with affordability and higher fuel prices cited. Parts and service revenue is recurring and supported by an average vehicle age of 13.0 years, and finance and insurance is tied to retail units while TCA defers commission revenue over contract terms, which depresses reported finance and insurance revenue during the rollout.

Costs are mostly variable through commissions but not fully: personnel costs fell with gross profit while rent and system costs did not, so selling, general and administrative expense reached 68.6% of gross profit. Free cash flow after capital expenditure was USD 369.7 million in the nine months, against USD 518.9 million, and 2026 capital expenditure guidance of USD 250.0 million to USD 275.0 million leaves some flexibility if earnings fall further.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 54, 60; calculation C3; calculation C9
### Competitive forces and external factors

Rivalry among franchised dealers is intense but inventory comes on equal terms, so margin is set by volume and mix; direct sales by some electric vehicle makers circumvent state franchise laws and are a substitution threat to the new vehicle line only. Buyers can compare prices easily, which caps new vehicle margins, and manufacturers hold the strongest supplier power through allocation, incentives and floor plan assistance of USD 79.4 million for nine months 2026, which the company says it cannot assume will continue.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_abg_abg-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 15–16; 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 62

Tariffs, higher fuel prices tied to 2026 conflicts, the expiry of federal electric vehicle incentives on September 30, 2025 and interest rates matter to credit: USD 1.94 billion of variable-rate debt including floor plan means a 100 basis point change moves annual interest by USD 19.4 million, partly hedged by swaps. Credit-supportive factors are scale, a service-led mix and owned property; credit-constraining factors are margin compression, leverage above target and refinancing concentration; improvement would come from stabilised new vehicle margins, and weakening from tariff-driven price increases that cut demand.
### Outlook

Over twelve to 24 months new vehicle margins and volumes are the swing factor, with parts and service growth and the unwinding of TCA commission deferral as partial offsets: deferred revenue of USD 891.3 million will be recognised over contract lives, which supports later finance and insurance revenue while depressing it now. The medium-term outlook beyond three years is not established because the filings give no projections beyond capital expenditure and the tax rate, and the sector commentary is qualitative.
### Downside scenario

The initiating condition is a further softening of new vehicle demand and margins from higher prices and weaker affordability, as in the third quarter of 2026 when new vehicle gross profit fell 20%. The first operational break is gross profit per new vehicle; because personnel, rent and system costs do not fall in step, income from operations and EBITDA drop faster than revenue. If EBITDA fell again by the USD 104.4 million already lost since year-end with net debt unchanged, net leverage would rise from 3.92x to 4.47x and interest cover would fall from 2.93x to 2.56x. Management levers are to keep buybacks paused against USD 322.4 million of remaining authorization, trim capital expenditure from the USD 250.0 million to USD 275.0 million plan, and sell further stores as it did for USD 397.2 million in nine months 2026. Company-defined liquidity of USD 1,031.9 million is 2.57 times the December 2026 maturity of USD 401.7 million, so a liquidity crisis does not appear likely within twelve months, but covenant headroom at the higher leverage cannot be established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_abg_abg-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9, 36, 55–56, 60; calculation C2; calculation C11; calculation C12
### Overall credit view

Overall, Asbury presents an adequate business profile supported by a service-led profit mix, brand and regional breadth and owned property, but credit quality is constrained by falling earnings, net leverage of 3.92x and a nearest maturity of USD 401.7 million that is not yet refinanced. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because parts and service and finance and insurance supply most gross profit, although free cash flow is lower than a year ago. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on the willingness of real estate lenders and the bank group to renew secured and floor plan lines, and on noteholders in 2028 to 2030. The primary downside path is margin compression in new vehicles feeding through a fixed cost base into leverage and cover. Further analysis would require the credit agreement and covenant levels, the company's leverage computation for September 2026, ratings and market prices, and any financing completed after October 30, 2026. Completed. Top risk: earnings decline on a largely fixed cost base while refinancing is pending.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C1; calculation C5; calculation C6
